lesson.title: Ancient Alliance: How Mitochondria Power the Eukaryotic Cell
lesson.summary: Mitochondria are double-membraned organelles that generate most of a cell's ATP through aerobic respiration, and strong evidence suggests they descend from free-living bacteria engulfed by an ancestral eukaryotic cell.
lesson.body:
Mitochondria are often introduced as the powerhouse of the cell, and while that phrase is a bit of a cliche, it captures something true: mitochondria are the primary site where eukaryotic cells convert the chemical energy stored in food molecules into ATP, the molecule cells use to power most of their energy-requiring activities. This process, called aerobic respiration, requires oxygen and is dramatically more efficient at extracting usable energy from glucose than the oxygen-independent processes available to a cell without mitochondria.

Structurally, a mitochondrion is bounded by two separate membranes rather than one. The outer membrane is smooth and relatively permeable, while the inner membrane is folded into numerous invaginations called cristae, which dramatically increase its surface area. This extra surface area matters because the inner membrane is where the electron transport chain sits, a series of protein complexes that pass electrons from one to the next, using the energy released to pump hydrogen ions across the membrane. Those hydrogen ions then flow back down their concentration gradient through a protein called ATP synthase, spinning it like a molecular turbine and driving the production of ATP, a process called chemiosmosis. The fluid-filled space enclosed by the inner membrane, called the matrix, contains the enzymes of the citric acid cycle, which breaks down the products of earlier metabolic steps and generates the electron carriers that feed into the electron transport chain.

One of the most compelling stories in cell biology concerns where mitochondria came from. According to the endosymbiotic theory, mitochondria descend from free-living, oxygen-using bacteria that were engulfed by a larger ancestral cell more than a billion years ago. Rather than being digested, the bacterium survived inside its host in a mutually beneficial relationship, eventually becoming a permanent, inherited feature of that lineage's descendants. Several lines of evidence support this theory. Mitochondria contain their own small, circular loop of DNA, structurally similar to the circular chromosomes found in bacteria rather than the linear chromosomes housed in the eukaryotic nucleus. They also contain their own ribosomes, which are closer in size and structure to bacterial ribosomes than to the ribosomes found elsewhere in the eukaryotic cytosol. Mitochondria reproduce by a splitting process resembling bacterial binary fission, on their own schedule somewhat independent of when the rest of the cell divides, and they are enclosed by two membranes, consistent with an origin as a free-living cell engulfed by a host membrane.

Not every cell invests equally in mitochondria, and that variation tells you something about what a cell does. Skeletal muscle cells and liver cells, both of which have high and sustained energy demands, contain far more mitochondria than cells with lower metabolic needs. This variability echoes a pattern seen throughout the eukaryotic cell: organelle abundance tracks with function, whether that organelle is rough ER in a secretory cell or mitochondria in a metabolically demanding one. Because mitochondria are membrane-bound organelles with their own genome, they also stand as one of the clearest illustrations of what compartmentalization made possible once eukaryotic cells evolved, an internal division of labor so effective that an entire independent organism was, in essence, absorbed and repurposed as permanent cellular machinery.
